text: No single security control is perfect. Firewalls get misconfigured, antivirus misses new malware, and employees click phishing links no matter how much training they've had. Defense in depth is the practice of building security as a series of independent, overlapping layers, so when any one layer fails, the attacker still has to get through the others before anything is actually compromised.

A mature security program stacks these layers from the outside in: a perimeter firewall filtering traffic at the network edge, network segmentation limiting how far an attacker can move once inside, endpoint protection on the actual device catching what got past the first two, access control and least privilege limiting what a compromised account can touch, and monitoring and logging as the detection layer underneath everything else.

Picture a phishing email that gets an employee to click a malicious link. The perimeter firewall doesn't block it — it looks like ordinary web traffic. Network segmentation means the employee's compromised machine still can't directly reach the finance servers on a separate VLAN. Endpoint protection flags the malicious file's behavior and quarantines it. Even if it partially executes, least privilege means that account never had domain admin rights to begin with. And monitoring catches the unusual connection attempt the next morning, when every automated layer has already done its part.

Buying ten firewalls isn't defense in depth — that's one layer, repeated, with the same blind spot. Real defense in depth means the layers fail for different reasons: a bad firewall rule doesn't also break endpoint detection, and one employee falling for phishing doesn't also disable network segmentation. That independence is what makes the whole system resilient even though every individual piece of it is imperfect.

That's the philosophy behind every policy and control in this chapter — each one is meant to be another independent layer, never the only layer. Next up: the written security policies, like acceptable use and password policy, that actually drive those technical controls in the first place.
